newsitem.title: USA: Dade County, Fla., upholds Smith Barney ouster.
newsitem.headline: Dade County, Fla., upholds Smith Barney ouster.

text.p: Florida's Dade County Commission on Tuesday upheld county Mayor Alex Penelas' decision to remove Smith Barney Inc from a bond deal because of concerns about the firm's conduct.
Smith Barney, a unit of Travelers Group Inc., had been chosen senior manager for a $124 million airport revenue refunding bond sale slated for late April.
Penelas vetoed the selection on March 7, saying a Securities and Exchange Commission investigation into Smith Barney's handling of a 1994 Dade County bond issue had "placed a cloud over the firm."

There was no motion to override the veto, which would have required a two-thirds vote of the commission. Instead, the commission amended the underwriter selection ordinance for the deal, removing Smith Barney but keeping syndicate members Goldman Sachs & Co, Bear Stearns & Co and Douglas James Securities Inc.
Bear Stearns was named senior manager. Instead of replacing Smith Barney, its share of the bonds are to be divided among the remaining syndicate members.
Smith Barney's removal was upheld despite assurances from the financial adviser for the deal that leaving them as senior manager would not affect bond pricing.

Smith Barney, in our opinion, by being senior manager in this transaction would not in any way affect the credibility of the deal or the market for the bonds," said Barry Kutun, a director at First Southwest Co, the financial adviser. "That is not the issue."
He said the decision to keep or remove them was one of policy, not pricing, and should be left to the commission.

Commissioner Jimmy Morales, who chairs the commission's finance committee, said Smith Barney should be ousted because the SEC investigation involved Dade County's own bonds. He said the probe focused on allegations that the firm misrepresented the county's potential savings in the 1994 deal, which involved a water-sewer refunding.

"Do we still want to do business with someone about whom we have questions ethically, legally, morally?" Morales said. "The allegation at least -- and the SEC doesn't investigate willy-nilly -- is perhaps they did something to this county."

Smith Barney officials were not immediately available for comment and did not address the commission Tuesday. The firm previously said it did not believe the probe would affect its ability to act as senior manager "consistent with the highest professional standards."
The revised ordinance that was approved Tuesday incorporated Penelas' request that the county issue new requests for proposals and choose all new underwriters, bond counsel and financial advisers.
There was no discussion of when that would be done. The county uses a standing pool of underwriting teams and bond counsel, assigning deals and choosing senior managers on a rotating basis.
The aviation bond deal marked the first time the county has asked underwriters to complete a disclosure questionnaire listing all pending litigation and regulatory probes.
"We want to make sure they are as un-dirty as possible," Morales said.
Smith Barney's reply, which said the firm was in discussions with the SEC about "a possible resolution" of the Dade probe, led to its ouster.

Morales said that did not necessarily mean all firms under SEC investigation would be barred from Dade deals. He acknowledged that it was difficult for large firms with offices nationwide to keep a tight rein on all its employees' actions. However, he said, the Smith Barney case deserved special attention because it involved Dade bonds.
"We have not adopted a firm standard. We are dealing with this on a case-by-case basis," Morales said.
